blocks.p: When the Prince had thus far remodeled the town of Mansoul, and had taught them what was profitable for them to know, he appointed another day on which he meant to bestow a further badge of honor on the town: a badge that would distinguish them from all the peoples, kindreds, and tongues that live in the kingdom of Universe. When the day came, the Prince and his people met in the King’s palace. There Emmanuel first made them a short speech, and then did for them as he had said, and to them as he had promised.
“My Mansoul,” he said, “what I am now about to do is to make you known to the world as mine, and to set you apart, in your own eyes too, from all false traitors who may creep in among you.”

Then he commanded his attendants to bring out of his treasury those white and glistening robes “that I,” he said, “have provided and stored up for my Mansoul.” So the white garments were fetched and laid out before the people. And they were given leave to put them on, “according,” he said, “to your size and stature.” So the people were dressed in white, in fine linen, white and clean.

Then the Prince said to them, “This, Mansoul, is my livery, the badge by which my own are known from the servants of others. Yes, it is what I give to all who are mine, and without it no one is allowed to see my face. Wear these robes, then, for my sake, who gave them to you; and wear them too if you want the world to know that you are mine.”
But now, can you imagine how Mansoul shone? It was fair as the sun, clear as the moon, and terrible as an army with banners. [Song 6:10]
The Prince went on: “No prince, ruler, or mighty one in Universe gives this livery but I. So, as I said before, by it you will be known to be mine.
“Now that I have given you my livery, let me also give you commands concerning it; and pay close attention to my words.

“First, wear them every day, so that you never appear to others as though you were not mine. Second, keep them always white; for if they are soiled, it is a dishonor to me. Third, therefore, gird them up off the ground, and do not let them trail in the dust and dirt. Fourth, take care not to lose them, or you will walk naked, and others will see your shame.

“Fifth, if you should soil them, if you should defile them (which I am very unwilling you should do, and which Prince Diabolus would be glad to see you do), then hurry to do what is written in my law, so that you may still stand, and come off well before me and before my throne. This is also the way to make sure that I do not leave you or forsake you while you are here, but may dwell in Mansoul forever.”

And now Mansoul and its inhabitants were like the signet ring on Emmanuel’s right hand. Where was there now a town, a city, a corporation, that could compare with Mansoul! A town redeemed from the hand and from the power of Diabolus! A town that King Shaddai loved, and that he sent Emmanuel to win back from the prince of the infernal cave; yes, a town that Emmanuel loved to live in, and that he chose for his royal dwelling; a town he fortified for himself and made strong with the force of his army! What more shall I say? Mansoul now has a most excellent Prince, golden captains and soldiers, tested weapons, and garments as white as snow. Nor are these benefits to be counted small, but great. Will Mansoul value them so, and put them to the use for which they were given?

When the Prince had thus completed the remodeling of the town, to show that he took great delight in the work of his hands, and pleasure in the good he had done for the famous and flourishing Mansoul, he had his standard set on the battlements of the castle. And then:

First, he visited them often. Not a day passed now but the elders of Mansoul must come to him in his palace, or he to them. Now they must walk and talk together of all the great things he had done, and had promised yet to do, for the town. He would often do this with the Lord Mayor, Lord Willbewill, the honest Mr. Conscience, the town’s own preacher, and Mr. Recorder. But oh, how graciously, how lovingly, how courteously and tenderly this blessed Prince now behaved toward the town of Mansoul! In all the streets, gardens, orchards, and other places where he went, you may be sure the poor would have his blessing; yes, he would kiss them, and if they were ill he would lay hands on them and make them well. The captains too he would encourage daily, sometimes hourly, with his presence and good words. For a smile from him would put more vigor, more life, and more courage into them than anything else under heaven.

The Prince would now also feast them and be with them continually; hardly a week would pass without a banquet between him and them. You may remember that some pages back we mentioned one feast they had together; but now feasting them was a common thing. Every day was a feast day with Mansoul now. Nor, when they went back to their homes, did he send them away empty: they must have a ring, a gold chain, a bracelet, a white stone, or something; so dear was Mansoul to him now, so lovely was Mansoul in his eyes.

Second, when the elders and townsmen did not come to him, he would send them provisions in great plenty: meat that came from the court, wine and bread prepared for his Father’s table. Yes, he would send them such delicacies, covering their table so richly that whoever saw it confessed that the like could not be seen in any kingdom.

Third, if Mansoul did not visit him as often as he wanted them to, he would walk out to them, knock at their doors, and ask to come in, so that their friendship might be kept up. If they heard and opened to him, as they commonly would if they were at home, he would renew his former love, and confirm it too with some new tokens and signs of his continued favor.

And was it not amazing to see now that in the very place where Diabolus had once lived, and entertained his Diabolonians almost to the utter destruction of Mansoul, the Prince of princes should sit eating and drinking with them, while all his mighty captains, soldiers, and trumpeters, with the singing men and singing women of his Father, stood around to wait on them! Now Mansoul’s cup ran over; now her conduits ran with sweet wine; now she ate the finest of the wheat, and drank milk and honey out of the rock! Now she said, “How great is his goodness! For since I found favor in his eyes, how honored I have been!”

The blessed Prince also appointed a new officer in the town, and a goodly person he was; his name was Mr. God’s-Peace. This man was set over Lord Willbewill, the Lord Mayor, Mr. Recorder, the town’s own preacher, Mr. Mind, and all the natives of Mansoul. He himself was not a native, but had come with Prince Emmanuel from the court. He was a close acquaintance of Captain Credence and Captain Good-Hope; some say they were kin, and I am of that opinion too. This man, as I said, was made governor of the town in general, and especially of the castle, and Captain Credence was to help him there. And I took careful note that as long as everything in Mansoul went as this sweet-natured gentleman wished, the town was in a most happy condition. There was no quarreling now, no scolding, no meddling, no unfaithful dealing in all Mansoul; every man kept close to his own work. The gentry, the officers, the soldiers, and everyone in authority kept to their order. And as for the women and children of the town, they went about their business joyfully; they would work and sing, work and sing, from morning till night; so that throughout Mansoul nothing was to be found but harmony, quietness, joy, and health. And this lasted all that summer.

But there was a man in the town of Mansoul whose name was Mr. Carnal-Security; and after all this mercy had been bestowed on the corporation, this man brought Mansoul into great and grievous slavery and bondage. Here is a brief account of him and his doings.

When Diabolus first took possession of Mansoul, he brought with him a great number of Diabolonians, men of his own kind. Among these was one named Mr. Self-Conceit, as notable and brisk a man as any who held Mansoul in those days. Diabolus, seeing that this man was active and bold, sent him on many desperate errands, which he managed better, and more to his lord’s liking, than most who came with him from the dens. So Diabolus promoted him and made him second only to the great Lord Willbewill, of whom we have written so much before. And Lord Willbewill, well pleased with him and his achievements, gave him his daughter, the Lady Fear-Nothing, to be his wife. And by Lady Fear-Nothing, Self-Conceit fathered this gentleman, Mr. Carnal-Security. So, since there were such strange mixtures in Mansoul then, it was hard in some cases to tell who were natives and who were not; for Mr. Carnal-Security sprang from Lord Willbewill on his mother’s side, though his father was a Diabolonian by nature.

Well, this Carnal-Security took much after his father and mother. He was self-conceited, he feared nothing, and he was also a very busy man. No news, no doctrine, no change or talk of change could ever be afoot in Mansoul but you could be sure Mr. Carnal-Security would be at the head or the tail of it. But he would always steer clear of the side he judged weakest, and stand with the side he supposed strongest.

Now when Shaddai the mighty and Emmanuel his Son made war on Mansoul to take it, this Mr. Carnal-Security was in the town, and was a great doer among the people, encouraging them in their rebellion and urging them to harden themselves in resisting the King’s forces. But when he saw that Mansoul was taken and turned over to the use of the glorious Prince Emmanuel; when he saw too what had become of Diabolus, and how he had been driven off his roost and made to quit the castle in the greatest contempt and scorn; and when he saw that the town was well stocked with captains, engines of war, and men, and provisions too; what did he do but slyly wheel around as well? And as he had served Diabolus against the good Prince, so now he pretended that he would serve the Prince against his enemies.

Having picked up a smattering of Emmanuel’s things, and being bold, he ventured into the company of the townsmen and tried to chat among them. Now he knew that Mansoul’s power and strength were great, and that the people could not fail to be pleased if he praised their might and glory. So he began his tale with the power and strength of Mansoul, and declared that it was impregnable: now extolling their captains and their slings and their battering rams; then praising their fortifications and strongholds; and lastly the assurances they had from their Prince that Mansoul should be happy forever. And when he saw that some of the men of the town were tickled and taken with his talk, he made it his business to go from street to street, house to house, and man to man, until at last he had brought Mansoul to dance to his pipe, and to grow almost as carnally secure as himself. So from talking they went to feasting, and from feasting to sporting, and so on to some other matters.

Now Emmanuel was still in Mansoul, and he wisely observed what they were doing. The Lord Mayor, Lord Willbewill, and Mr. Recorder were all taken with the words of this chattering Diabolonian gentleman as well. They forgot that their Prince had warned them before to take care that they were not deceived by any Diabolonian trick. He had told them, besides, that the security of the now flourishing town of Mansoul lay not so much in her present fortifications and forces as in using what she had so as to oblige her Emmanuel to stay within her castle. For the right doctrine of Emmanuel was that Mansoul should take care not to forget his Father’s love and his, and should so conduct themselves as to keep themselves in it. And this was not the way to do it: to fall in love with one of the Diabolonians, and with such a one as Mr. Carnal-Security at that, and to be led up and down by the nose by him. They should have heard their Prince, feared their Prince, loved their Prince, and stoned this worthless rascal to death, and taken care to walk in the ways their Prince had prescribed. For then their peace would have been like a river, and their righteousness like the waves of the sea. [Isa. 48:18]
Now when Emmanuel saw that through the scheming of Mr. Carnal-Security the hearts of the men of Mansoul had grown cold, and their practical love for him had dwindled, this is what he did.

First, he lamented over them and grieved over their state with the Secretary, saying, “Oh, if only my people had listened to me, and Mansoul had walked in my ways! I would have fed them with the finest of the wheat, and with honey out of the rock I would have satisfied them.” [Ps. 81:13-16] Having said this, he said in his heart, “I will return to the court and go to my place, until Mansoul considers and acknowledges their offense.” [Hos. 5:15] And he did so. He went because Mansoul had first turned away from him, as these particulars make plain.
1. They gave up their former habit of visiting him; they did not come to his royal palace as before.
2. They did not care, or even notice, whether he came to visit them or not.
3. As for the love feasts that used to be held between their Prince and them, though he still made them and invited them, they neglected to come, or to take any delight in them.

4. They did not wait for his counsel, but began to be headstrong and self-confident, concluding that they were now strong and invincible, that Mansoul was secure and beyond all reach of the enemy, and that her state must necessarily remain unchanged forever.

Now, as I said, when Emmanuel saw that the cunning of Mr. Carnal-Security had drawn Mansoul away from depending on him, and on his Father through him, to trust instead in the gifts they had bestowed on it, he first lamented their state, and then took steps to show them that the way they were going was dangerous. For he sent the Lord High Secretary to them to forbid them such ways. But twice when he came to them he found them at dinner in Mr. Carnal-Security’s parlor; and seeing, too, that they were unwilling to reason about their own good, he was grieved and went his way. When he told this to Prince Emmanuel, the Prince took offense, and was grieved too, and so made arrangements to return to his Father’s court.
Now the manner of his withdrawing, as I was saying before, was this:
1. Even while he was still with them in Mansoul, he kept to himself and was more withdrawn than before.
2. When he came into their company, his speech was no longer as pleasant and familiar as it used to be.
3. Nor did he send to Mansoul from his table those choice morsels he used to send in times past.

4. Nor, when they came to visit him, as now and then they would, was he as easy to speak with as they had found him before. They might knock once, or even twice, but he would seem not to notice them at all; whereas formerly, at the sound of their feet, he would get up and run to meet them halfway, and take them and hold them close to his heart.

By this behavior Emmanuel sought to make them think again and return to him. But alas, they did not consider; they did not know his ways; they paid no attention; they were not moved by these things, nor by any true remembrance of past favors. So what did he do but quietly withdraw himself, first from his palace, then to the gate of the town, and so away from Mansoul he went, until they should acknowledge their offense and seek his face more earnestly. Mr. God’s-Peace also laid down his commission, and for the present would act no longer in the town of Mansoul.

So they walked contrary to him, and he in turn walked contrary to them. But alas, by this time they were so hardened in their way, and had drunk in the doctrine of Mr. Carnal-Security so deeply, that the departure of their Prince did not touch them; they did not remember him when he was gone, and so, of course, did not mourn his absence.

Now there came a day when this old gentleman, Mr. Carnal-Security, made another feast for the town. There was at that time in Mansoul a certain Mr. Godly-Fear, a man now little thought of, though once in great demand. Old Carnal-Security had a mind, if possible, to dupe and corrupt and abuse him as he had the rest, so he invited him to the feast with his neighbors. When the day came, he took his place among the other guests. When they were all seated, they ate and drank and were merry, all except this one man; for Mr. Godly-Fear sat like a stranger, and neither ate nor was merry. When Mr. Carnal-Security noticed this, he at once spoke to him.

“Mr. Godly-Fear, aren’t you well? You seem to be ill in body or mind, or both. I have a cordial of Mr. Forget-Good’s making; if you’ll take a dram of it, sir, I hope it will make you bright and cheerful, and so fitter company for us feasters.”

The good old gentleman replied discreetly, “Sir, I thank you for everything courteous and civil; but I have no wish for your cordial. But a word to the natives of Mansoul. You, the elders and chief men of Mansoul: it seems strange to me to see you so jolly and merry when the town of Mansoul is in such a sorry state.”
“You need sleep and good air, I suspect,” said Mr. Carnal-Security. “If you like, lie down and take a nap, and meanwhile we’ll be merry.”
“Sir,” said the good man, “if you were not without an honest heart, you could not do what you have done, and are doing.”
“Why?” said Mr. Carnal-Security.

“No, please don’t interrupt me. It is true that Mansoul was strong, and, on one condition, impregnable. But you, the townsmen, have weakened it, and now it lies open to its enemies. Nor is this a time to flatter, or to keep silent. It is you, Mr. Carnal-Security, who have craftily stripped Mansoul and driven her glory from her. You have pulled down her towers, you have broken down her gates, you have spoiled her locks and bars.

“And now, to explain myself: from the time that my lords of Mansoul and you, sir, became so intimate, from that time the Strength of Mansoul has been offended; and now he has risen up and is gone. If anyone questions the truth of my words, I will answer him with questions like these: Where is Prince Emmanuel? When did any man or woman in Mansoul last see him? When did you last hear from him, or taste any of his choice morsels? You are feasting now with this Diabolonian monster, but he is not your Prince. I say, therefore, that though enemies from outside could never have made a prey of you if you had taken care, yet since you have sinned against your Prince, your enemies within have been too strong for you.”

“Shame, shame, Mr. Godly-Fear, shame!” said Mr. Carnal-Security. “Will you never shake off your timidity? Are you afraid a sparrow will strike you down? Who has hurt you? Look, I am on your side; only you are for doubting, and I am for being confident. Besides, is this a time to be sad? A feast is made for mirth. Why, then, to your shame and our trouble, do you break out into such gloomy, overwrought talk, when you should eat and drink and be merry?”

“I may well be sad,” said Mr. Godly-Fear again, “for Emmanuel is gone from Mansoul. I say again, he is gone, and you, sir, are the man who has driven him away. Yes, he has gone without so much as telling the nobles of Mansoul of his going; and if that is not a sign of his anger, I know nothing of the ways of godliness.

“And now, my lords and gentlemen, for my speech is still to you: your gradual turning away from him provoked him to depart from you gradually. This he did for some time, in case you might be brought to your senses by it, and be renewed by humbling yourselves. But when he saw that no one would pay attention, or take these fearful beginnings of his anger and judgment to heart, he went away from this place; and I saw it with my own eyes. So now, while you boast, your strength is gone. You are like the man who had lost the locks that once waved about his shoulders. You may, with this lord of your feast, shake yourselves and expect to do as at other times; but since without him you can do nothing, and he has departed from you, turn your feast into sighing and your mirth into lamentation.”
Then the town’s own preacher, old Mr. Conscience, who had once been Recorder of Mansoul, was startled at what was said, and began to back it up.

“Indeed, my brothers,” he said, “I fear Mr. Godly-Fear is telling us the truth. For my part, I have not seen my Prince for a long time. I cannot remember the day, nor can I answer Mr. Godly-Fear’s question. I fear, I am afraid, that all is wrong with Mansoul.”

“No,” said Mr. Godly-Fear, “I know you will not find him in Mansoul, for he has departed and is gone; yes, and gone for the faults of the elders, because they repaid his grace with unbearable unkindness.”

Then the preacher looked as though he would fall down dead at the table; and everyone present, except the man of the house, began to look pale and wan. But when they had recovered themselves a little, and had agreed together to believe Mr. Godly-Fear, they began to consult about what was best to be done, both with the man of the house, for drawing them into evil, and to recover Emmanuel’s love. (Mr. Carnal-Security had gone off into his withdrawing room by now, for he did not like such gloomy goings-on.)

And with that, a saying of their Prince came burning into their minds: what he had told them to do to such false prophets as should arise to deceive the town of Mansoul. So they seized Mr. Carnal-Security (concluding that he must be one of them) and burned his house down on top of him; for he too was a Diabolonian by nature.

When this was over and done, they hurried out to look for Emmanuel their Prince; and they sought him, but they did not find him. Then they were all the more convinced that Mr. Godly-Fear had spoken the truth, and they began to reflect severely on themselves for their vile and ungodly doings; for they concluded now that it was because of them that their Prince had left them.

Then they agreed to go to the Lord Secretary (the one they had refused to hear before, the one they had grieved by their doings) to learn from him, since he was a seer, where Emmanuel was, and how they might direct a petition to him. But the Lord Secretary would not admit them to a conference about the matter, nor let them into his royal dwelling, nor come out to them to show them his face or give them any word.

And now it was a gloomy and dark day, a day of clouds and of thick darkness for Mansoul. Now they saw that they had been foolish, and began to see what the company and prattle of Mr. Carnal-Security had done, and what desperate damage his swaggering words had brought poor Mansoul into. But what it was likely to cost them further, they did not know. Now Mr. Godly-Fear began to be held in respect again by the men of the town; yes, they were ready to look on him as a prophet.

Well, when the Sabbath came, they went to hear their town’s own preacher. But oh, how he thundered and lightened that day! His text was that saying in the prophet Jonah: “Those who cling to empty lies forsake their own mercy.” [Jonah 2:8] There was such power and authority in that sermon, and such dejection to be seen on the faces of the people that day, that its like has seldom been heard or seen. When the sermon was over, the people were scarcely able to get to their homes, or to set about their work the week after; they were so sermon-smitten, and so sermon-sick from being smitten, that they did not know what to do.

He did not only show Mansoul their sin; he trembled before them under the sense of his own, crying out against himself as he preached to them: “Unhappy man that I am! That I should do so wicked a thing! That I, a preacher, whom the Prince set up to teach Mansoul his law, should myself live here senseless and stupefied, and be one of the first found in transgression! And this transgression fell within my own district. I should have cried out against the wickedness; but I let Mansoul lie wallowing in it until it had driven Emmanuel from its borders!” And with these things he also charged all the lords and gentry of Mansoul, until they were almost out of their minds.
